claimBoundary: This is one provenance-bound Codex pass. It is single-model evidence, not human, instructor, independent, classroom, or multi-judge validation.

claims: A list is an ordered collection of values written in square brackets; each element has an index, beginning at 0.
A list is written with square brackets [] holding comma-separated values.
Individual elements are accessed directly using an index.
Indexes begin at 0 and end at one less than the length of the sequence.
A for loop can iterate through a list, visiting each element in order.
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §3.4 List basics; §9.1 Modifying and iterating lists

artifact.q: A student stores quiz scores as 12, 15, and 18 in one Python sequence. Which notation matches a list of those scores?
artifact.ex: [12, 15, 18] is correct because a list is written with square brackets holding comma-separated values. The parenthesized choice is a tuple-shaped misconception, while braces suggest a different container.

artifact.q: If a list has a length of 5, what is the highest valid index for an element?
op: 5 (since indexing starts at 1)
4 (since indexes end one less than length)
6 (since indexes start at 0)
5 (since indexes begin at 0)
artifact.ex: Indexes begin at 0 and end at one less than the length of the sequence.

claims: A class defines a type of object with attributes (data) and methods (behavior); it is a blueprint, and each object built from it is an instance.
A class is a blueprint for creating objects.
Individual objects created from a class are called instances.
Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes, while the methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §11.1 Object-oriented programming basics; §11.2 Classes and instances

artifact.q: A student writes a class for `Rocket`. Which claim best matches what a class does in Python?
op: It defines a type of object with data and behavior.
It is one object copied into every program.
It stores only method names, not data.
It is the same thing as an instance.
artifact.ex: Correct: a class is a blueprint that defines a type of object with attributes and methods. A common misconception is that the class itself is one finished object; that would describe an instance, not the blueprint.

artifact.q: How are individual objects created from a class referred to?
op: A instances
B blueprints
C attributes
D methods
artifact.ex: Individual objects created from a class are called instances. This distinguishes them from the class itself.

claims: File I/O lets a program read information from and write information into files; a file is accessed by opening it, working with its contents, and closing it.
open() returns a file object that the program then reads from or writes to.
read() reads the entire contents of a file and returns a single string.
readline() returns the next single line, while readlines() returns a list with every line of the file.
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §14.1 Reading from files

artifact.df: The data structure returned by the open() function that allows interaction with the file.
artifact.eg: Using the file object to call read() to get a string from the file.
artifact.mi: Thinking the file object is the file itself, rather than the handle to the file.
artifact.cx: The file object is the program's interface for reading or writing file contents.

artifact.df: A way for a program to work with data stored in files by opening the file, using its contents, and then closing it.
artifact.eg: A student script opens a text file of survey answers, reads the lines, and then closes the file.
artifact.mi: It only means saving information, not reading it.
artifact.cx: It includes both reading from files and writing into files.

claims: Geologic time spans the roughly 4.5-billion-year history of Earth; relative dating orders events by which is older or younger, while absolute dating assigns numerical ages in years.
Absolute (numerical) dating assigns specific ages in years to mineral grains within a rock.
By the principle of superposition, in an undisturbed sequence the bottom layers are oldest and the upper layers younger.
By original horizontality, sediments and lava flows are laid down horizontally, so tilted layers were disturbed after deposition.
The Earth is about 4.54 billion years old, and this vastness of geologic time allowed life to evolve.
attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §7.1 Relative dating and geologic time

artifact.df: A method that assigns a specific numerical age in years to material from a rock.
artifact.eg: Measuring zircon grains and reporting an age such as 2.1 billion years.
artifact.mi: It only tells whether one layer is above or below another.
artifact.cx: That is relative dating; absolute dating gives a year-based age.

artifact.df: Ordering events based on which is older or younger.
artifact.eg: Determining that a layer of sediment is older than the layer above it.
artifact.mi: Confusing relative dating with absolute dating, believing relative terms imply specific year counts.
artifact.cx: Relative dating orders events by which is older or younger.

claims: Metamorphic rock forms when heat, pressure, and fluids change a preexisting parent rock (the protolith) in the solid state, without melting it.
Metamorphism changes a solid rock's composition and texture without the mineral crystals melting.
The starting rock that undergoes metamorphism is called the parent rock, or protolith.
Directed stress aligns mineral crystals into planes, producing foliation.
attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §6.1 Metamorphism and metamorphic rocks

artifact.df: Change in a solid rock caused by heat, pressure, and fluids without melting.
artifact.eg: A buried shale becoming a metamorphic rock while remaining solid.
artifact.mi: It requires the rock to melt first.
artifact.cx: The correction is that the mineral crystals stay solid during the change.

artifact.df: The initial rock subjected to metamorphic change.
artifact.cx: The starting rock that undergoes metamorphism.

claims: In music, form refers to the structure of a musical composition or performance.
The term "binary form" is used to describe a musical piece with two sections that are about equal in length.
Musical form unfolds over time through the expansion and development of these ideas.
Form in music is the result of the interaction of the four structural elements described above [sound, harmony, melody, rhythm].
Subdivisions of each large musical unit are shown by lowercase letters (a, b, and so on).
The next level concerns the entire structure of any single self-contained musical piece or movement.

artifact.df: The organized structure of a composition or performance.
artifact.eg: A self-contained movement can be examined as its sections unfold over time.
artifact.mi: It means only the melody line.
artifact.cx: It also involves the interaction of sound, harmony, melody, and rhythm.

artifact.df: The overall arrangement of a musical composition or performance.
artifact.eg: Analyzing the entire structure of a single movement.
artifact.mi: A specific melodic line or chord progression.
artifact.cx: The overall structure of any single self-contained musical piece or movement.

claims: In music, harmony is the concept of combining different sounds in order to create new, distinct musical ideas.
In these genres, chord progressions are the defining feature on which melody and rhythm are built.
Chord progressions are the foundation of harmony in Western musical tradition from the common practice era of classical music to the 21st century.
A first chord forms a 'progression' with a second chord, and a second with a third.
For example, the relative minor of C major is A minor, and in the key of A minor, the i, iv and v chords are A minor, D minor and E minor.
In many styles of popular and traditional music, chord progressions are expressed using the name and "quality" of the chords.

artifact.df: The specific role or quality assigned to a chord within a progression, often expressed by its name.
artifact.eg: Identifying the i, iv, and v chords in the key of A minor.
artifact.mi: Assuming all chords in a progression share the same function.
artifact.cx: Understanding that chord function dictates the harmonic relationship between chords in a progression.

artifact.df: A sequence in which one chord leads to another and then to another.
artifact.eg: A move from one chord to a second, then a third, as the source describes.
artifact.mi: It is the same thing as melody or rhythm.
artifact.cx: The packet says progressions are a foundation for harmony, while melody and rhythm are built on them in some genres; that keeps the roles distinct.

claims: In music theory, an interval is a difference in pitch between two sounds.
In physical terms, an interval is the ratio between two sonic frequencies.
Intervals between successive notes of a scale are also known as scale steps.

artifact.q: What is the primary definition of an interval in music theory?
op: A) The ratio between two sonic frequencies.
B) The difference in pitch between two sounds.
C) The ratio between two sonic frequencies and two sounds.
D) The difference in pitch between two sounds and scale steps.
artifact.ex: Option B is correct because an interval is defined as the difference in pitch between two sounds (claims[0]). Option A is a physical description, not the primary theoretical definition. Option C combines two distinct concepts. Option D incorrectly conflates intervals with scale steps.

artifact.q: A student hears two notes and asks for the interval in the most basic music-theory sense. Which description fits best?
op: The difference in pitch between the two sounds
The chord built from those two notes
The pattern made by repeating the notes in order
The overall form of the passage
artifact.ex: Correct: an interval is the pitch difference between two sounds. The most plausible misconception is to treat the interval as a chord or a larger formal pattern, but those describe harmony or form, not the relation between just two pitches.

claims: Interactive prototyping builds a testable representation of how a planned experience looks and works without requiring every production detail.
Prototypes can be combined with usability testing or a cognitive walkthrough to test whether a design concept works.
Functional prototypes allow a team to observe how users interact with a product.
A prototype should show the major interactions even when not every interaction is functional.
Prototypes should support fast iteration and be inexpensive enough to discard after learning from them.

artifact.df: Creating a testable stand-in for a planned experience before all production details are finished.
artifact.eg: A course team builds a clickable checkout mockup and runs a quick usability check on it.
artifact.mi: It is the same as a finished product.
artifact.cx: It is a learning tool, not a final release, so it can be incomplete and still useful.

artifact.df: A model used to verify an experience's viability.
artifact.eg: A low-fidelity wireframe used to test the main navigation flow.
artifact.mi: A representation that includes every production detail.
artifact.cx: A representation that shows how an experience looks and works without needing every production detail.

claims: A UX research plan turns a decision need into actionable learning objectives, participants, tasks, evidence-capture roles, and a rehearsal-ready study setup.
The team should agree what it wants to learn from the research round before selecting study details.
A prototype used in research should work end-to-end and be usable and accessible in the research venue.
Researchers should run through test tasks on the day before the research session.
A practice session with a team member can expose procedure problems before participants arrive.

artifact.q: What should the team establish prior to selecting study details?
op: The specific evidence capture roles
The desired learning objectives
The rehearsal-ready study setup
The specific tasks
artifact.ex: Selecting study details should follow agreement on what the team wants to learn from the research round. Choosing the specific tasks is premature before defining the learning goals.

artifact.q: What preparation best supports a research session for a prototype being tested with users?
op: Ensure the prototype works end-to-end and is usable and accessible in the venue.
Add extra features so participants can explore beyond the task.
Delay practice until after the first participant finishes.
Use a partial mockup if the final screens are not ready.
artifact.ex: Correct: the prototype should work end-to-end and be usable and accessible in the research venue. The most plausible misconception is that a partial mockup is enough for testing; the source says the prototype used in research should already function across the flow and fit the venue conditions.
